<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-nass-autoplot-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-nass-autoplot" width="80%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-nass-autoplot</p>
</div>

The dashed line is the model-averaged prediction over the retained equations and
the grey band its 95% credible interval. The band is narrow wherever a dose was
tested and opens across the interval from
1.25 to
2.5, where none was: the curve has to fall
somewhere in there and the data do not say where. The solid line is the
model-averaged *N(S)EC* and the dotted lines its bounds, at
0.31 and 1.92, which
between them span that untested interval. The axis is the one the raw-data
figure used, so the control keeps its marked position and the nine doses at or
below 1.25 are legible rather than stacked.


# A non-constant coefficient of variation {#a-non-constant-coefficient-of-variation}

Step 4 asked whether the fitted model reproduced the spread observed within each
concentration group, and on `simazine` it did. A third response is worked here,
on which it does not. This is the assumption a threshold estimate depends on
most, and the one no convergence diagnostic reports.

Every family with a free dispersion parameter holds that parameter constant
along the series unless the formula says otherwise. For a `Gamma` under the
identity link a constant `shape` is a constant coefficient of variation: the
standard deviation of a replicate is a fixed multiple of the fitted mean at
every concentration. Where replicate variation does not behave that way, one
`shape` is estimated as a compromise between the two ends of the series and
describes neither.

## The assay

The `lum31` data record acute copper and zinc toxicity tests run on the Lum-31
bioluminescent bacterial assay [@luter2025]. A suspension of marine bacteria is
dosed in a microplate well and its light output read after a fixed exposure, so
luminescence in relative light units is the response.

One plate of the copper series at 15 minutes is worked here. A plate is a
complete test of eleven concentrations by four replicate wells. The plate reader
sets its gain per read, so plates are not on a common vertical scale, and taking
one plate removes that difference rather than modelling it.
[*Grouping and factor covariates*](https://open-aims.github.io/bayesnec/articles/example8.html)
covers the group-level terms that handle the whole assay, and the left-censoring
that the blank correction requires.


``` r
data(lum31)
cu <- droplevels(subset(lum31, plate == "Cu 19Mar24 Rep1B" & minutes == 15))
c(wells = nrow(cu), concentrations = length(unique(cu$conc)),
  at_the_floor = sum(cu$censoring != "none"))
#>          wells concentrations   at_the_floor 
#>             44             11              1
```

It is one of two plates in the arm of
16 with
the fewest readings at the instrument's floor, which is one of 44. A reading held at a bound contributes a spread smaller than the one
the well would have shown, so a plate with many of them would understate exactly
the quantity this section is about.

Each concentration on one plate holds four wells, so a coefficient of variation
computed within a concentration involves no curve, and no lack of fit in the
mean can inflate it.


``` r
cv_obs <- tapply(cu$rlu_cens, cu$conc, function(z) sd(z) / mean(z))
round(cv_obs, 3)
#>     0.003 0.0137424  0.023888  0.044776  0.086552 0.1707008 0.3389984    0.6744    1.3458    2.6886 
#>     0.046     0.033     0.046     0.042     0.030     0.084     0.168     0.465     1.271     0.958 
#>    5.3742 
#>     0.876
```

It sits between 0.030 and
0.046 over the five lowest concentrations, then
rises without interruption to 1.271 at
1.3 mg/L, and eases
to 0.876 at the bottom of the series. The
largest of these is 28 times the control value. A
`Gamma` fitted with one `shape` returns a single value for all of it.

## Fitting and screening the set

The copper response falls from its control, so `decline` is the candidate set.
The zinc series in the same dataset rises above its control at low
concentrations and needs the hormesis equations as well, which is why the other
vignette fits `all` there.


``` r
gfam <- Gamma(link = "identity")
set_const <- bnec(rlu_cens | cens(censoring) ~ crf(log(conc), model = "decline"),
                  data = cu, family = gfam, seed = 17)
```


``` r
screened_const <- screen_models(set_const)
#> Dropping 2 of 11 candidate models that failed the sampler screen:
#>   -  nec4param: Rhat 1.018, ESS 36.1
#>   -  ecxll5: Rhat 1.022, ESS 185.6, 925 divergent transitions
#> Fitted models are: nec3param ecxexp ecx4param ecxwb1 ecxwb2 ecxwb1p3 ecxwb2p3 ecxll4 ecxll3
best_const <- pull_best(screened_const)
#> Highest-weighted model is ecxll4, holding 0.276 of the weight of 9 candidate models.
#> Pulling out model(s): ecxll4
```


``` r
copper_axis <- list(
  scale_x_continuous(transform = "log", breaks = c(0.003, 0.03, 0.3, 3),
                     labels = function(x) signif(x, 2)),
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) {
    format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
  }),
  labs(x = expression(paste("Copper (mg ", L^-1, ")")),
       y = "Relative light units")
)
autoplot(screened_const) + copper_axis
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-disp-autoplot-const-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-disp-autoplot-const" width="80%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-disp-autoplot-const</p>
</div>

The curve is the model-averaged prediction over the retained equations, with its
95% credible band and the model-averaged *N(S)EC* marked. The mean is described
well: the response holds above
91
per cent of its control value to
0.045 mg/L and falls to below one per
cent by 0.34.

The band is the part to look at. It is a credible interval on the *mean*, and at
the control it is several hundred thousand relative light units wide, against
four control wells that span
117,000
between the lowest and the highest. An interval on a mean that is wider than the
observations the mean was estimated from is what a dispersion parameter fitted
too large looks like once it reaches the curve. The rest of the section
establishes that this is what has happened, and what it does to the estimates.

14 equations were requested. `bnec_record()` reports
that 3 were excluded before fitting and
0 failed to fit, which on
44 observations is the five-parameter equation. The screen removed
2 more. Steps 2 and 3 cover all three
mechanisms.

## The probability integral transform

For a continuous response, the probability integral transform value of an
observation is the proportion of that observation's posterior predictive draws
falling at or below it. A model that is right about the location and the spread
of every observation produces values spread uniformly over the unit interval. A
model simulating more variability than the data contain produces values crowded
towards the middle, because an observation drawn from a narrower distribution
than the one simulated for it lands near the centre of those draws. A model
simulating less variability produces values crowded into the two ends.

`pp_check(type = "pit_ecdf")` plots the empirical distribution function of those
values against the uniform, between two dashed lines that a correctly specified
model stays inside with probability 0.99 over the whole interval at once.


``` r
pp_check(best_const, type = "pit_ecdf")
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-pit-const-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-pit-const" width="60%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-pit-const</p>
</div>


``` r
# pp_check() leaves the censored reading out, because the draws it compares it
# against are uncensored. The same subset is used here.
pit <- function(fit) {
  keep <- cu$censoring == "none"
  yrep <- posterior_predict(pull_brmsfit(fit))[, keep]
  colMeans(sweep(yrep, 2, cu$rlu_cens[keep], "<="))
}
pit_const <- pit(best_const)
round(c(middle_half = mean(pit_const > 0.25 & pit_const < 0.75),
        below_0.05 = mean(pit_const < 0.05),
        above_0.95 = mean(pit_const > 0.95)), 3)
#> middle_half  below_0.05  above_0.95 
#>       0.721       0.070       0.047
```

The curve runs along the lower dashed line from about 0.25 to 0.5, leaves it,
and crosses above the upper one beyond 0.6. That is the crowding towards the
middle described above:
0.721 of the values lie
in the middle half of the interval where 0.5 is expected. The fit simulates more
variability than the observations contain. The band is wide because it is drawn
for 43 observations, and the curve leaves it even so.

## The concentrations the variance is wrong at

The transform pools every observation, so it states that the calibration is
wrong and not where along the series it is wrong. `check_fit()` answers that,
by comparing the observed spread within each concentration against the spread
the fit simulates there. On one plate each of its groups is four wells at one
concentration, which is the same unit the coefficients of variation above were
computed on.


``` r
cf_const <- check_fit(best_const)
cf_const[, c("group", "n", "obs_sd", "sim_sd", "sd_ratio", "ppp_sd", "control")]
#>        group n    obs_sd     sim_sd sd_ratio ppp_sd control
#> 1      0.003 4 48659.995 532381.471    0.091  0.999    TRUE
#> 2  0.0137424 4 34254.508 527165.661    0.065  0.999   FALSE
#> 3   0.023888 4 45273.800 503326.230    0.090  0.999   FALSE
#> 4   0.044776 4 40495.610 516624.598    0.078  0.998   FALSE
#> 5   0.086552 4 23064.931 433730.559    0.053  1.000   FALSE
#> 6  0.1707008 4 14403.575  90827.189    0.159  0.997   FALSE
#> 7  0.3389984 4  1143.009   3354.690    0.341  0.944   FALSE
#> 8     0.6744 4   221.393    278.380    0.795  0.647   FALSE
#> 9     1.3458 4   251.933    193.239    1.304  0.305   FALSE
#> 10    2.6886 4   513.008    187.545    2.735  0.026   FALSE
#> 11    5.3742 4   297.087    189.093    1.571  0.208   FALSE
```

`sd_ratio` is the observed spread divided by the simulated one, so 1 is
agreement. It lies between
0.05 and
0.09 over the five lowest
concentrations, then rises to a maximum of
2.74 at
2.7
mg/L, and 7 of its
11 groups are flagged. The fit simulates about
11 times the spread the control
shows, and about 3 times too little where the
ratio is largest. One `shape` cannot do both, which is what a constant
coefficient of variation requires of it.

## The dispersion sub-model

`disp("power")` writes `log(shape)` as a linear function of `log(mu)`, so the
dispersion parameter becomes a function of the fitted mean rather than a
constant. [*Single model usage*](https://open-aims.github.io/bayesnec/articles/example1.html)
covers the variance functions available, the families each applies to, and what
the estimated exponent implies for a given family.


``` r
set_power <- bnec(rlu_cens | cens(censoring) ~ crf(log(conc), model = "decline") +
                    disp("power"),
                  data = cu, family = gfam, seed = 17)
```


``` r
screened_power <- screen_models(set_power)
#> Dropping 1 of 11 candidate models that failed the sampler screen:
#>   -  ecxwb1: Rhat 1.011, ESS 227.7
#> Fitted models are: nec3param nec4param ecxexp ecx4param ecxwb2 ecxwb1p3 ecxwb2p3 ecxll5 ecxll4 ecxll3
best_power <- pull_best(screened_power)
#> Highest-weighted model is ecxll5, holding 0.834 of the weight of 10 candidate models.
#> Pulling out model(s): ecxll5
```

The screen is run again rather than assumed. It removes
1 equation here, and not the same one it
removed before: a dispersion sub-model changes the posterior every equation is
sampled from. The same equation holds the most weight in both sets, and holds
more of it in this one. The weights themselves concentrate: under constant
dispersion 4 equations
share them, and under the sub-model
3 do.


``` r
brms::fixef(pull_brmsfit(best_power))[c("c0_Intercept", "c1_Intercept"), ]
#>              Estimate  Est.Error     Q2.5     Q97.5
#> c0_Intercept 4.775596 0.26582158 4.223835 5.2632690
#> c1_Intercept 0.788979 0.06528559 0.662953 0.9203914
```

`c1` is the exponent, and zero is the constant-dispersion model, so an interval
excluding zero reflects the data rather than the prior. The coefficients of
variation computed above give an estimate of the same quantity that uses no fit:
a power law makes `log(cv)` linear in `log(mu)` with slope `-c1/2`.


``` r
conc_mean <- tapply(cu$rlu_cens, cu$conc, mean)
obs_slope <- lm(log(cv_obs) ~ log(conc_mean))
# Multiplying by -2 reverses the order of the bounds, so the names confint()
# supplied would be attached to the wrong ends.
setNames(-2 * c(coef(obs_slope)[[2]], rev(confint(obs_slope)[2, ])),
         c("c1", "lower", "upper"))
#>        c1     lower     upper 
#> 0.7689298 0.6579071 0.8799526
c(r_squared = summary(obs_slope)$r.squared)
#> r_squared 
#> 0.9646321
```

The two agree. The fit gives
0.79
on an interval of
0.66
to
0.92,
and the wells give
0.77 on
0.66 to
0.88. The sub-model is therefore
describing the replicate variation the design measured, and not absorbing a
failure of the curve elsewhere in the series. No curve enters a
within-concentration standard deviation, which is what makes that comparison
worth making. Whether a power law is the right form for the relationship is a
separate question, and the regression answers it here with an R-squared of
0.965 on
9 degrees of freedom.


``` r
pp_check(best_power, type = "pit_ecdf")
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-pit-power-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-pit-power" width="60%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-pit-power</p>
</div>


``` r
pit_power <- pit(best_power)
round(c(middle_half = mean(pit_power > 0.25 & pit_power < 0.75),
        below_0.05 = mean(pit_power < 0.05),
        above_0.95 = mean(pit_power > 0.95)), 3)
#> middle_half  below_0.05  above_0.95 
#>       0.581       0.047       0.023
```

The curve stays between the dashed lines across the whole interval, and the
middle half holds
0.581 of the values
against the 0.5 expected, where the constant-dispersion fit put
0.721 there. The
transform is computed from draws, so on
43 observations its tail counts are themselves
noisy, and the middle half is the stable summary of the three.

## The check repeated within concentrations

A transform computed over the whole fit is a weaker requirement than a
comparison made within each group, so the group-wise check is run again as well.


``` r
cf_power <- check_fit(best_power)
c(flagged = sum(cf_power$ppp_sd > 0.95 | cf_power$ppp_sd < 0.05),
  groups = nrow(cf_power),
  control_sd_ratio = round(cf_power$sd_ratio[cf_power$control], 3))
#>          flagged           groups control_sd_ratio 
#>            0.000           11.000            1.155
```

0 of the
11 groups are flagged, against
7 before, and the control
is at 1.15 where it was
0.09. Both checks agree that
the sub-model corrected what the first one found.

`plot()` draws each statistic against the spread the fit simulates for it, and
takes both fits at once where a `model` column tells the panels apart. The
response falls from about
1,060,000
relative light units at the control to about
198
at the bottom, so the display is put on a logarithmic scale; on a linear one the
lower half of the series is a row of points on the axis.


``` r
both <- rbind(cbind(cf_const, model = "constant"),
              cbind(cf_power, model = "disp(\"power\")"))
class(both) <- class(cf_const)
plot(both) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = function(x) {
    format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
  })
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-disp-checkfit-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-disp-checkfit" width="92%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-disp-checkfit</p>
</div>

Each bar is the 95% span of the statistic simulated from the fit and each point
is the value observed. The location panels are the same under both, and every
observed mean lies inside its bar in each: the curve reproduces the response at
every concentration whichever dispersion structure is used, so the mean was
never what was wrong. The scale panels differ. Under constant dispersion the
observed standard deviation lies below its bar at the
6 concentrations where the response is highest,
and the gap at the control is more than an order of magnitude:
48,700
observed against a simulated span reaching
1,420,000.
Under the sub-model the bars close on the points and every observed standard
deviation lies inside its own, the control among them, at
48,700
against a span of
13,000
to
89,800.
A model can describe the mean of every group and still be wrong about the spread
of all of them, which is the case the Overview singles out, and it is the case
the sub-model corrects here.


``` r
sd_ratios <- rbind(cbind(cf_const, dispersion = "constant"),
                   cbind(cf_power, dispersion = "disp(\"power\")"))
# check_fit() returns the group as a character label, so it is converted back
# before it can be drawn on a concentration axis.
sd_ratios$conc <- as.numeric(sd_ratios$group)
ggplot(sd_ratios, aes(x = conc, y = sd_ratio, colour = dispersion,
                      shape = dispersion)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(transform = "log", breaks = c(0.003, 0.03, 0.3, 3)) +
  scale_y_continuous(transform = "log", breaks = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey35", "#1b6ca8")) +
  labs(x = expression(paste("Copper (mg ", L^-1, ")")),
       y = "Observed / simulated residual SD", colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-sdratio-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-sdratio" width="80%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-sdratio</p>
</div>

The constant-dispersion series climbs across three orders of magnitude of the
predictor, passing through agreement near
0.67
mg/L. The `disp("power")` series stays near the dashed line, and does not sit on
it: its ratios run from
0.61 to
1.94, and on a logarithmic axis the low
end is as far from agreement as the high end. None of those groups is flagged,
and the reason is the design rather than the fit. A standard deviation computed
from four values has a sampling standard deviation of about
41 per cent of
itself, so four wells do not resolve a spread more finely than that span. What
the display supports is that the ratios no longer trend with concentration, not
that each one is exactly 1.

## The reported estimates

The fit the estimates come from is the screened set under the sub-model, drawn
here with its credible band.


``` r
autoplot(screened_power) + copper_axis
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-autoplot-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-autoplot" width="80%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-autoplot</p>
</div>

The curve is the model-averaged prediction over the retained equations and the
band is its 95% credible interval, both returned on the recorded concentration
scale although the formula fitted `log(conc)`. The response holds above
91 per cent of its
control value to
0.045 mg/L, is at
16 per cent of it by
0.17, and below one per cent by
0.34, so the whole decline occupies
a factor of about
8 in
concentration. The vertical lines mark the model-averaged *N(S)EC* and its
bounds.

Set beside the constant-dispersion curve drawn earlier, the band has closed onto
the observations and the *N(S)EC* the figure annotates has fallen with it. The
two curves describe the same mean; what differs is how wide each makes the
posterior at the control, and that is measured below.

The diagnostics above are run on the highest-weighted equation, which is what
`pp_check()` and `check_fit()` take. The estimates are read from the screened
set, as step 5 does, because the weights here are spread across several
equations and no one of them describes the model-averaged value on its own.


``` r
round(summary(screened_const)$mod_weights[, "wi"], 3)
#> nec3param    ecxexp ecx4param    ecxwb1    ecxwb2  ecxwb1p3  ecxwb2p3    ecxll4    ecxll3 
#>     0.000     0.000     0.241     0.245     0.238     0.000     0.000     0.276     0.000
```


``` r
rbind(constant = nsec(screened_const, xform = exp),
      power = nsec(screened_power, xform = exp))
#>                 Q50       Q2.5      Q97.5
#> constant 0.10245262 0.04134296 0.13893236
#> power    0.04080062 0.02577804 0.05864743
rbind(constant = ecx(screened_const, ecx_val = 10, xform = exp),
      power = ecx(screened_power, ecx_val = 10, xform = exp))
#>                 Q50       Q2.5      Q97.5
#> constant 0.08304419 0.01579731 0.12044674
#> power    0.06359693 0.05757490 0.07261332
```

The *NSEC* falls from
0.102 to
0.041 mg/L, a factor of
2.5.
The mechanism is what `nsec()` reads its reference from, which is the posterior
of the control mean with any group-level deviation excluded.


``` r
control_reference <- function(fit) {
  nd <- data.frame(conc = min(cu$conc), censoring = "none")
  post <- posterior_epred(pull_brmsfit(fit), newdata = nd, re_formula = NA)[, 1]
  c(sd = sd(post), cv = sd(post) / mean(post),
    reference_share = unname(quantile(post, 0.01) / mean(post)))
}
round(rbind(constant = control_reference(best_const),
            power = control_reference(best_power)), 4)
#>                 sd     cv reference_share
#> constant 155326.81 0.1540          0.7089
#> power     13149.87 0.0129          0.9708
```

That posterior is
12
times wider under constant dispersion. `nsec()` sets its reference at a lower
quantile of it, so the reference sits at
0.71 of the
control mean there against
0.97 under the
sub-model. A reference placed that far below the control is crossed further
along the curve, so the constant-dispersion fit reports the *less* protective of
the two figures, and nothing in its sampler diagnostics says so.

EC10 changes by less, from
0.083 to
0.064 mg/L,
while its interval narrows from
0.105
to
0.015
mg/L. It is measured at a fixed fraction of the control mean rather than at a
quantile of its posterior, so the variance assumption reaches it through the
precision of the curve rather than through the placement of its reference. That
is the difference the Overview draws between the two.

A methods section states the dispersion structure each estimate was fitted
under, because the two structures return different estimates from the same data.

# Summary

The sampler screen returned a different outcome at each of the three fits, and
none of them was predictable before it was run. On `simazine` at deliberately reduced settings it removed 3 of 11 equations; at `bnec()`'s defaults on the same data it removed 0 of 11, with a further equation failing to fit at all; and on `nassarius` at those same defaults it removed 8 of 10. That is the argument for running and reporting the screen in every case.

The three outcomes have three different causes, and separating them is what the
step is for. An equation that fails on effective sample size alone has not been
given enough draws, and the remedy is to give it more. An equation that fails on
divergent transitions, or that fails to fit at all, is reporting something about
the posterior. Where it is also the most heavily parameterised equation in the
set and the design has few distinct concentrations, the explanation is that the
experiment does not contain the information it needs. Adjusting the settings
further to retain it is not the right response. An equation that fails at the cutoff is a
decision the analyst has taken, and it has to be reported as one.

The variance assumption is the one no sampler diagnostic reports. On the
`lum31` copper plate the observed coefficient of variation ran from
0.046 at the control to
0.876 at the bottom of the series, and the
constant-dispersion fit passed the sampler screen while simulating about
11 times the spread the control
shows. Adding `disp("power")` brought every group inside the flag and halved
the model-averaged *NSEC*, from
0.102 to
0.041 mg/L. A fit can pass every
check the sampler screen applies and still simulate the wrong spread at the
concentration both estimators are referenced from.

The same holds one level up. The dispersion screen returned `binomial` because it
detected nothing, not because nothing was there; the family for a continuous
bounded response was settled by the support of the data and not by a test; and
estimates are reported on the scale they were fitted on unless `xform` says
otherwise. None of those is a result the workflow produces automatically. Each is
a decision the analysis has to record.
